primitives.name: Anchored Kickout Movement
primitives.verbatim_quote: Furthermore, we analyze the movement of the shooter and his defender and find that more than half of these shots involve a shooter anchored at the corner waiting for the kick out pass.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'P(anchored)': 'Probability of shooter being stationary for ≥4 seconds (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Offense runs pick-and-roll or ball-screens to generate passing angles; defense fails to rotate quickly enough to the corner.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Static shooter creates predictable timing windows; defender must choose between guarding the catch or helping on the roll.

layer2.mapping: GSI: Hidden Markov Model for player trajectory classification. GSE: Semi-Markov decision process with observation delays.
layer2.telemetry: Average anchor time in corner before shot, pass completion rate from interior zones to corner.

primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'p_c': 'Probability defender commits to corner shooter (dimensionless)', 'p_d': 'Probability defender helps at basket (dimensionless)', 'x': 'Mixed strategy probability of committing (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Two-player zero-sum game; uniform distribution of offensive play types; static defender positioning.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Pure strategies lead to exploitable patterns; mixed strategy prevents opponent from predicting next move.

layer2.telemetry: Defender positioning variance between corner and paint, transition probabilities between guarding modes.

reasoning_traces.think:
Corner threes exploit the geometric chokepoint where the arc meets the baseline, forcing defenders into a binary choice: guard the stationary corner shooter or provide help defense at the rim. The anchored kickout movement creates a predictable timing window, allowing the offense to establish a favorable shooting environment. The resulting defensive commitment tradeoff leads to reduced contest intensity, explaining the observed 38.8% field goal success rate despite the 23-foot distance. This primitive reveals that optimal defensive schemes must incorporate dynamic rotations and probabilistic coverage rather than rigid man-to-man assignments.
